title: Wolstenholme Primes and the Mod 4 Question
description: A Wolstenholme prime p has C(2p-1,p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p⁴). Only two known: 16843 and 2124679, both ≡ 3 (mod 4). Proves small primes are not Wolstenholme, both known WPs are ≡ 3 (mod 4), and formalizes the open question of whether a WP ≡ 1 (mod 4) exists.

overview.historicalContext:
Joseph Wolstenholme proved in 1862 that $\binom{2p-1}{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^3}$ for all primes $p \geq 5$, strengthening an earlier result of Charles Babbage (1819) who had established the mod $p^2$ version. A prime satisfying the even stronger congruence modulo $p^4$ is called a **Wolstenholme prime**, a concept introduced and studied by Richard McIntosh.

McIntosh discovered the first Wolstenholme prime, $p = 16843$, in 1995 through systematic computation of Bernoulli numbers — specifically by checking which primes satisfy $p \mid B_{p-3}$, an equivalent characterization. The second, $p = 2124679$, was found by McIntosh and E. L. Roettger in 2007 using a refined search algorithm. Their exhaustive computation up to $10^9$ confirmed these are the only two below that bound.

The mod 4 pattern is tantalizing: $16843 \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ and $2124679 \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$. Finer analysis reveals $16843 \equiv 3 \pmod{8}$ and $2124679 \equiv 7 \pmod{8}$ (different mod 8 classes), yet both share $p \equiv 7 \pmod{12}$. Whether there exists a Wolstenholme prime $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ remains open, with no theoretical obstruction known in either direction. The question connects to irregular prime theory (via $p \mid B_{p-3}$) and to the broader study of arithmetic properties of exceptional primes (Wieferich, Wall-Sun-Sun, Fibonacci-Wieferich).
overview.problemStatement:
**Open Question**: Does there exist a Wolstenholme prime $p$ with $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$?

A Wolstenholme prime is a prime $p$ such that:
$$\binom{2p-1}{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^4}$$

The only known Wolstenholme primes are 16843 and 2124679, both $\equiv 3 \pmod{4}$.
overview.text: Formalizes Wolstenholme primes and the open question of whether any is ≡ 1 (mod 4). Proves primes 5-23 are not Wolstenholme, both known WPs are ≡ 3 (mod 4), and establishes logical equivalences between the open question and the all-mod-3 conjecture.
overview.proofStrategy:
The formalization takes a three-pronged approach:

1. **Computational exclusion**: Using `native_decide`, we verify that every prime from 5 to 23 fails the mod $p^4$ test. This establishes a large computational gap before the first Wolstenholme prime.

2. **Known examples**: The two known Wolstenholme primes 16843 and 2124679 are axiomatized (binomial coefficients too large for the kernel), while their primality is verified computationally.

3. **Residue analysis**: We prove both known WPs are $\equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ (and analyze finer residues mod 8 and mod 12), then formalize the open question and its logical equivalence with the conjecture that all WPs are $\equiv 3 \pmod{4}$.
keyInsights: Every Wolstenholme prime must be at least 5 (and hence odd): primes 2 and 3 fail the mod $p^4$ test computationally, and 0, 1, 4 are not prime
The two known Wolstenholme primes 16843 ≡ 3 (mod 8) and 2124679 ≡ 7 (mod 8) cover different mod 8 classes, both mapping to 3 (mod 4)
Both known WPs share the same residue mod 12: $16843 \equiv 2124679 \equiv 7 \pmod{12}$, possibly hinting at a deeper structural constraint
The AllWPMod3 conjecture is logically equivalent to ¬WPMod1Exists: the open question has a clean dichotomy with no middle ground
Any third Wolstenholme prime must exceed $10^9$ by the McIntosh-Roettger computational search, making empirical investigation extremely expensive

**Bernoulli number characterization**: A prime $p$ is Wolstenholme iff $p \mid B_{p-3}$, connecting to irregular prime theory. This links the binomial coefficient condition to the deep arithmetic of Bernoulli numbers and Kummer's criterion for regularity

**Computational methodology**: The formalization uses `native_decide` for small primes but axiomatizes the two known WPs because $\binom{33685}{16842}$ has thousands of digits — beyond the Lean kernel's practical computation limit

sections.title: Core Definitions
sections.summary: Central binomial coefficient cb(p) = C(2p-1, p-1) and IsWP predicate.
sections.mathContext: A Wolstenholme prime is a prime p where C(2p-1, p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p⁴), strengthening Wolstenholme's theorem which gives mod p³.

sections.title: Structural Properties
sections.summary: Every WP is ≥ 5, odd, and either 1 or 3 mod 4.
sections.mathContext: Eliminates small cases computationally (native_decide for p=2,3) and by primality (decide for p=0,1,4). Since p ≥ 5 and prime, p is odd.

sections.title: Small Primes Are NOT Wolstenholme
sections.summary: Computational proof that primes 5 through 23 fail the mod p⁴ test.
sections.mathContext: native_decide computes C(2p-1,p-1) mod p⁴ and verifies it differs from 1 for p = 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23.

sections.title: The Two Known Wolstenholme Primes
sections.summary: 16843 and 2124679 are Wolstenholme primes (primality by native_decide, mod p⁴ values axiomatized).

sections.title: Residue Analysis
sections.summary: Both known WPs are ≡ 3 (mod 4), with finer analysis mod 8 and mod 12.

sections.title: The Open Question
sections.summary: WPMod1Exists and AllWPMod3 are mutually exclusive conjectures; their equivalence is proved.
sections.mathContext: AllWPMod3 ↔ ¬WPMod1Exists: every WP is 1 or 3 mod 4 (since odd), so ruling out mod 1 forces all to be mod 3, and vice versa.

sections.title: Computational Lower Bound
sections.summary: Any third WP exceeds 10⁹ (from McIntosh-Roettger search).
sections.mathContext: Axiomatized: no WP below 10⁹ other than 16843 and 2124679. Corollary: a new WP must be ≥ 10⁹.

sections.title: Connection to Wolstenholme's Theorem
sections.summary: Every WP satisfies the ordinary Wolstenholme theorem (mod p³) via divisor chain.
sections.mathContext: p³ | p⁴ and n % p⁴ = 1 imply n % p³ = 1. Uses Nat.mod_mod_of_dvd.

conclusion.summary: This formalization establishes the framework for studying Wolstenholme primes and their residue properties. It combines computational verification (native_decide) with axiomatic statements from the literature to prove that both known Wolstenholme primes are ≡ 3 (mod 4), and formalizes the open question as a clean logical dichotomy.
conclusion.implications:
The open question connects to several areas:

1. **Quadratic residues**: Both known WPs have 2 as a quadratic non-residue (p ≡ 3, 7 mod 8), which constrains the arithmetic structure

2. **Bernoulli numbers**: Wolstenholme primes are characterized by p | B_{p-3}, connecting to irregular prime theory

3. **Computational search**: Any resolution requires examining primes beyond 10⁹, making this a challenge for large-scale computation
openQuestions: Does there exist a Wolstenholme prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4)?
Are there infinitely many Wolstenholme primes?
Is there a theoretical explanation for why the known WPs are both ≡ 3 (mod 4)?

crossReferences.description: Extends Wolstenholme's theorem ($\binom{2p-1}{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^3}$ for $p \geq 5$) to study the stronger mod $p^4$ condition defining Wolstenholme primes. Every WP satisfies the parent theorem as a divisibility consequence

Both Wilson's theorem ($(p-1)! \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$) and Wolstenholme's theorem concern mod $p^k$ congruences for factorial/binomial expressions. Wilson characterizes primes via factorials; Wolstenholme strengthens this to mod $p^3$ for central binomials

The binomial coefficient $\binom{2p-1}{p-1}$ (the central object of this formalization) arises from the binomial expansion. Properties of binomial coefficients underpin both Wolstenholme's theorem and its mod $p^4$ strengthening

Kummer's theorem characterizes the $p$-adic valuation of binomial coefficients via base-$p$ carry counting. It provides the theoretical framework for understanding when $p^k \mid \binom{n}{m}$, which is central to the Wolstenholme prime condition $p^4 \mid \binom{2p-1}{p-1} - 1$
